quotes.t: What is the hardest thing of all? That which seems easiest for your eyes to see, that which lies before your eyes.
If a man knows not to which port he sails, no wind is favorable.
The best thing about the future is that it comes one day at a time.
One must wait until the evening to know how splendid the day has been.
You are the sky. Everything else — it's just the weather.
To study the Buddha Way is to study the self.
It is dangerous to be right in matters on which the established authorities are wrong.
The darker the night, the brighter the stars.
Hope is the thing with feathers that perches in the soul.
quotes.source: Hope is the thing with feathers

quotes.t: The unexamined life is not worth living.
You don't have to be great to start, but you have to start to be great.
You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with.
Remember, today is the tomorrow you worried about yesterday.
The most precious gift we can offer others is our presence. When mindfulness embraces those we love, they will bloom like flowers.
When we are mindful, deeply in touch with the present moment, our understanding of what is going on deepens, and we begin to be filled with acceptance, joy, peace and love.
Two souls, alas, dwell in my breast.
What you have inherited from your fathers, earn it in order to possess it.
For what is prayer but the expansion of yourself into the living ether?
The mind that is anxious about future events is miserable.
The one who plants trees, knowing that he will never sit in their shade, has at least started to understand the meaning of life.
I do not think much of a man who is not wiser today than he was yesterday.
The educated differ from the uneducated as much as the living from the dead.
Man is by nature a political animal.
It is possible to fail in many ways, while to succeed is possible only in one way.
Never argue with stupid people, they will drag you down to their level and then beat you with experience.
Success is liking yourself, liking what you do, and liking how you do it.
There is more to life than increasing its speed.
True friends stab you in the front.
Life is too important to be taken seriously.
Respect Buddha and the gods without counting on their help.
A fanatic is one who can't change his mind and won't change the subject.
We are all worms, but I do believe that I am a glow worm.
I never worry about action, but only about inaction.
No pessimist ever discovered the secret of the stars, or sailed to an uncharted land, or opened a new doorway for the human spirit.
Although the world is full of suffering, it is full also of the overcoming of it.
Creativity is seeing the same thing but thinking differently.
All the powers in the universe are already ours.
Take risks in your life. If you win, you can lead. If you lose, you can guide.
We know the truth, not only by the reason, but also by the heart.
Everything will be okay in the end. If it's not okay, it's not the end.
Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake.
Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, in front of the essential facts of life.
We live in a wonderful world that is full of beauty, charm and adventure.
The measure of a man is what he does with power.
Let us read, and let us dance; these two amusements will never do any harm to the world.
The soul is healed by being with children.
I am made and remade continually. Different people draw different words from me.
We don't see things as they are, we see them as we are.
Dreams are necessary to life.
Permanence, perseverance and persistence in spite of all obstacles, discouragements, and impossibilities: It is this, that in all things distinguishes the strong soul from the weak.
No pressure, no diamonds.
I cannot teach anybody anything. I can only make them think.
If you can dream it, then you can achieve it.
Discipline is the bridge between goals and accomplishment.
Do the hard jobs first. The easy jobs will take care of themselves.
Understanding is love's other name.
You may give them your love but not your thoughts, for they have their own thoughts.
And ever has it been that love knows not its own depth until the hour of separation.
I am not in this world to live up to your expectations and you are not in this world to live up to mine.
A quick temper will make a fool of you soon enough.
Wrinkles should merely indicate where the smiles have been.
We cannot change anything until we accept it. Condemnation does not liberate, it oppresses.
Show me a sane man and I will cure him for you.
We all should know that diversity makes for a rich tapestry, and we must understand that all the threads of the tapestry are equal in value no matter what their color.
Poverty is the worst form of violence.
There is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about.
You can be sure of succeeding in your attacks if you only attack places which are undefended.
Do not hold on to possessions you no longer need.
Do not act following customary beliefs.
When one door of happiness closes, another opens; but often we look so long at the closed door that we do not see the one which has been opened for us.
You get in life what you have the courage to ask for.
He who loves practice without theory is like the sailor who boards ship without a rudder and compass.
A winner is a dreamer who never gives up.
I am prepared for the worst, but hope for the best.
It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.
The snake which cannot cast its skin has to die. As well the minds which are prevented from changing their opinions; they cease to be mind.
Change your opinions, keep to your principles; change your leaves, keep intact your roots.
Fiction is the lie through which we tell the truth.

In everyone's life, at some time, our inner fire goes out. It is then burst into flame by an encounter with another human being. We should all be thankful for those people who rekindle the inner spirit.
Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?'
If I loved you less, I might be able to talk about it more.
There is nothing like staying at home for real comfort.
The brain is wider than the sky.
The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes.
Into each life some rain must fall.
She walks in beauty, like the night of cloudless climes and starry skies.
We are interested in others when they are interested in us.
Chance is always powerful. Let your hook be always cast.
While there's life, there's hope.
Death is nothing to us.
I can't go back to yesterday because I was a different person then.
In politics, stupidity is not a handicap.
Be not afraid of growing slowly, be afraid only of standing still.
Nothing ever goes away until it teaches us what we need to know.
God is a comedian playing to an audience too afraid to laugh.
It is not the brains that matter most, but that which guides them — character, heart, generous qualities, progressive ideas.
People often say that motivation doesn't last. Well, neither does bathing. That's why we recommend it daily.
He who climbs upon the highest mountains laughs at all tragedies, real or imaginary.
To learn to read is to light a fire; every syllable that is spelled out is a spark.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Abraham Lincoln.bio: 16th president of the United States (1861-1865), who led the country through the Civil War and abolished slavery.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Aristotle.bio: Greek philosopher and student of Plato; founder of logic and many scientific fields.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.
Bruce Lee.credit: National General Pictures, Public domain (File: File:Bruce Lee 1971 National General Pictures publicity photo.jpg)

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Epicurus.bio: Epicurus was a Greek philosopher who founded a school in Athens known as the Garden. He taught that pleasure, rightly understood as freedom from pain and fear, comes from friendship, simplicity and philosophy rather than luxury.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German writer, poet, playwright and natural philosopher, regarded as Germany's greatest literary figure. His works include the drama Faust, The Sorrows of Young Werther and Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.credit: Joseph Karl Stieler, Public domain (File: Goethe (Stieler 1828).jpg)

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Kahlil Gibran.bio: Lebanese-American writer and poet, best known for The Prophet (1923), one of the best-selling books of all time.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Lewis Carroll.bio: English writer and mathematician, author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

Lord Byron.bio: English Romantic poet known for Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Rabindranath Tagore.bio: Bengali poet and polymath from India; the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913), known for Gitanjali.

Seneca.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman, author of Letters to Lucilius.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thich Nhat Hanh.bio: Vietnamese Buddhist monk and peace activist who popularized mindfulness in the West; nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr.
Thich Nhat Hanh.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 (File: File:Hòa thượng Ấn Kim - Tổ Tuân - Hoằng Tịnh. 印 金 祖 恂 弘 净.jpg)

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

William James.bio: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist, regarded as a founder of modern psychology and a leading thinker of pragmatism. His works include The Principles of Psychology (1890), The Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
